intro_en: The Israel National Trail runs along the Yarkon River: from its mouth at the sea to the sources of the Yarkon, the Rosh HaAyin springs and Tel Afek.
character_en: Easy walking, partly shaded along the banks of the Yarkon
transport_en: Bus stops near the Yarkon, next to the Reading parking lot. The Petah Tikva - Rosh HaAyin road, not far from Tel Afek
pois_en: Tel Aviv Port. Yarkon Park and the Yarkon River. Abu Rabah Mill. The Concrete House (Beit HaBeton). Mir Mill, the Water Lily Pool. Tel Afek
important_en: Bathing in the Yarkon River is prohibited, but east of its confluence with Nahal Kana (south-east of the Hod HaSharon Ecological Park) there is a popular bathing spot.
description_en:
The route begins at the mouth of the Yarkon by the sea, and heads east up the Yarkon, against the direction of the water's flow.
The starting point is on the southern bank of the Yarkon, on the northern edge of the Tel Aviv Port compound. After a short distance, the trail crosses a footbridge to the northern bank of the river and into the expanses of Yarkon Park, with its lawns and sports and leisure facilities.
Along the way we encounter remains and evidence of the days when the Yarkon served as a source of energy to power flour mills: the sites of Seven Mills (Sheva Tahanot) and Ten Mills (Eser Tahanot). Assuta Hospital in Ramat HaHayal, located near the trail, marks the exit from the urban area.
Until the crossing of Road 4, we walk on dirt roads surrounded by reeds. Immediately after passing under the road bridge, an area of citrus groves begins.
The trail continues to follow the winding course of the Yarkon (whose Arabic name is Auja, 'the winding one'). We cross bridges over tributaries that flow into the Yarkon from the north, the first of which is Nahal Hadarim. Immediately afterwards, the trail 'cuts' a meander of the Yarkon, shortening our way almost without our noticing.
Further on we pass under Road 5 and over the streams Nahal Pardes and Nahal Hadar. Near the confluence with Nahal Hadar, the orange-marked 'Sharon Trail' branches off and crosses the Sharon via Beit Berl, Tel Mond and Nahal Alexander to Michmoret.
A short walk north along the Sharon Trail brings you to Hod HaSharon Park, a recreation and leisure site with a lake at its centre, which offers drinking water and toilets, and usually also a pizza and coffee truck. The lake water is treated wastewater from the surrounding towns. Israel National Trail hikers are welcome to camp and sleep on the lawns in the park.
After crossing Nahal Hadar, the trail continues along the bank of the Yarkon through tunnels of reeds. The trail crosses the 'Farukhiya Mill' bridge to the southern bank of the Yarkon. After the crossing, we proceed along a white dirt road parallel to Road 5; a tall electricity pylon beside the trail marks the point where the trail turns back north, to the banks of the Yarkon. We reach a lovely spot for a break: Abu Rabah Mill, a historic flour mill building inside a large meander of the river.
The trail continues on the northern bank through tunnels of reeds, up to the crossing point of Road 40. After the crossing, the trail passes between large eucalyptus trees on the right and farm fields on the left; beyond the fields we can see the outskirts of Hod HaSharon. The trail passes an abandoned two-storey building, Beit Leah, a historic citrus-grove house from the 19th century. Beside the building, among the eucalyptus trees, is a lovely spot for a break and a rest on the banks of the Yarkon.
We continue walking on the northern bank, which within a short walk becomes the eastern bank of the river because of the change in the channel's direction. In the next section, the Yarkon flows from south to north.
We cross under Road 5 via a bridge and continue to a footbridge that takes us to the western bank, near the Concrete House (Beit HaBeton), a historic building erected in the early 20th century, when concrete construction had only just arrived in the country.
Further on, the trail moves away from the Yarkon channel, skirts the Baptist Village and enters the Yarkon Sources (Mekorot HaYarkon) National Park through the ticket booths. Inside the national park, the trail passes the 'Mir Mill', the remains of a flour mill that operated on the bank of the Yarkon, and continues along the Yarkon.
After leaving the park, we pass under the railway line that connects Petah Tikva and Rosh HaAyin. Next to the railway bridge you can see a pillbox, a structure used during the British period to guard the bridge.
We cross the Yarkon on a footbridge; the trail continues alongside a green fence at the foot of the railway embankment. When we see a gate in the fence on the right with a sign beside it, it is worth going in for a short visit to the Water Lily Pool (Breikhat HaNufarim), a spot where yellow water lilies grow on the banks of the Yarkon. These are aquatic plants whose leaves float on the water and form a green carpet. In summer we can see the water lilies blooming yellow.
The trail continues to Tel Afek National Park, along the Einat Canal, an artificial channel that has been restored and creates a water-rich environment that attracts wildlife and plants typical of wetland habitats, which have almost disappeared from Israel because of human activity. In this section water flows in the canal all year round.
We enter Tel Afek National Park through a pedestrian gate on the western side of the park and cross it to the park's main entrance gate. Inside the park, we pass alongside an artificial lake, at the foot of Tel Afek, a mound that throughout history served as a point of control over the Afek Pass, the passage that allowed travellers to bypass, from the east, the springs and marshes that surrounded the Yarkon. The park's entrance gate is the end point of the segment.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
